name: Confractosuchus
sum: Basal eusuchian from the Cenomanian Winton Formation of Australia, preserved with a juvenile ornithopod dinosaur in its stomach.
wsnote: The skull is 28.5 cm long and 19 cm wide; the sources give no body length. The cervical vertebrae are unfused, so the holotype was a sub-adult.
holotype: Largely articulated, crushed skeleton lacking most of the pelvis, hind limbs and tail, with stomach contents — upper Winton Formation, central-western Queensland, Australia (White et al. 2022).
material: One specimen, found in 2010 in a concretion while sauropod bones were being excavated; osteoderms were preserved with it but not in articulation.
exceptional: Partly digested bones (vertebrae and limb bones) of a juvenile ornithopod dinosaur, probably about 1.7 kg, in the abdomen; revealed by neutron tomography.
biology: The skull shape suggests a macro-generalist able to take prey larger than itself, probably an opportunistic feeder rather than a dinosaur specialist. The preserved meal is the first evidence of a crocodyliform eating a dinosaur, and the state of the bones suggests the prey had been dismembered as living crocodilians do. All paravertebral osteoderms were single-keeled, so the back armour was fully segmented and more flexible in the water than the tightly interlocking armour of goniopholids and pholidosaurids. Some vertebrae are procoelous and others amphicoelous, which may mark a transitional condition.
author: White et al. 2022

sources.text: White, M.A.; Bell, P.R.; Campione, N.E.; Sansalone, G.; Brougham, T.; Bevitt, J.J.; Molnar, R.E.; Cook, A.G.; Wroe, S.; Elliott, D.A. 2022. Abdominal contents reveal Cretaceous crocodyliforms ate dinosaurs. Gondwana Research 106: 281–302. doi:10.1016/j.gr.2022.01.016
